title: Strategy Pattern
oneLiner: Makes an algorithm swappable at runtime by putting each variant behind the same interface.

hero.name: Shape-Shifter
hero.catchphrase: Same job, different move — pick your algorithm.
hero.power: Swaps an entire algorithm in or out at runtime, without the code that uses it ever changing.
hero.weakness: A handful of nearly-identical strategies with one-line differences is its own kind of clutter — sometimes a parameter would've done the job.
hero.origin: Shape-Shifter appeared inside a shipping calculator's 400-line if/else chain, one branch per carrier's pricing algorithm, that grew every quarter.

story.problem: `calculateShipping()` has a giant if/else chain: one branch per carrier's pricing algorithm. Every new carrier means editing this one increasingly fragile function.
story.solution: Shape-Shifter gives each carrier its own `ShippingStrategy` implementation. `calculateShipping()` just calls `strategy.calculate(cart)` — it doesn't know or care which carrier it is.
story.result: Adding a carrier means adding one new strategy class. The core shipping code never changes again.

before: One giant if/else chain, one branch per algorithm
Adding an algorithm means editing shared code
Hard to test one pricing algorithm in isolation
after: Each algorithm is its own swappable class
Adding an algorithm means adding one new file
Each strategy is trivially testable on its own

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: calculateShipping() has grown to a 400-line if/else chain, one branch per carrier.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're adding a fifth carrier and I have to touch this massive function again. One typo breaks all four existing carriers.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Shape-Shifter appears, morphing between four different forms.
panels.speaker: Shape-Shifter
panels.dialogue: Stop branching on carrier inside one function. Give each carrier its own algorithm — and let the caller just swap which one it uses.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Each carrier implements the same ShippingStrategy interface. calculateShipping() just calls strategy.calculate().
panels.speaker: Shape-Shifter
panels.dialogue: The caller doesn't know or care which strategy it's holding. Swap it out entirely, and nothing else changes.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The fifth carrier ships as a new 15-line file. The 400-line function is gone entirely.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One new file, fully tested in isolation, zero risk to the other four carriers.

useWhen: You have several interchangeable algorithms for the same task and need to pick one at runtime.
A function's conditional logic branches heavily on 'which algorithm' — that's a strong Strategy smell.
You want each algorithm to be independently testable without dragging in the others.
avoidWhen: There's only one algorithm and no realistic need for a second — the interface is pure overhead.
The 'algorithms' differ by a single parameter — a config value is simpler than a whole class.
The number of near-identical strategies grows large enough that the class count becomes its own maintenance burden.
commonMistakes: Reaching for Strategy when a single parameterized function would solve the same problem more simply.
Leaking algorithm-specific details back into the caller, defeating the point of swappability.
Not giving the caller an easy way to choose a strategy (hardcoding one strategy negates the pattern's benefit).
Confusing Strategy with State — Strategy is chosen by the client; State transitions are driven by the object itself.
explanation.realWorldExample: Sorting functions that accept a custom comparator, payment processing that swaps between providers, and compression libraries that let you pick gzip vs. brotli vs. zstd are all Strategy in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Couldn't I just pass a function instead of a whole Strategy class?

conversation.speaker: Shape-Shifter
conversation.message: In many languages, absolutely — a function IS a lightweight Strategy. I matter most when the algorithm needs its own state or several related methods, not just one function signature.

conversation.speaker: Shape-Shifter
conversation.message: When your 'strategies' are one line each and differ only by a number. That's a parameter, not a pattern.

codeBattle.scenario: Your image export feature needs to support PNG, JPEG, and WebP compression, each with a completely different algorithm, chosen by the user at export time.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Shape-Shifter lets the export feature swap between fully independent compression algorithms at runtime, chosen by the caller, with no shared conditional logic.

quiz.question: What is the core problem Strategy solves?
options: Conditional logic that branches heavily on 'which algorithm to use' becomes hard to maintain and extend
An object needs to notify many listeners of a change
A complex object needs to be constructed step by step
Two incompatible interfaces need to work together
quiz.answer: Conditional logic that branches heavily on 'which algorithm to use' becomes hard to maintain and extend
quiz.explanation: Strategy's entire purpose is replacing that branching with swappable, independently testable algorithm objects.

quiz.question: Who decides which Strategy is used?
options: The client code, which selects and supplies the strategy
It's fixed permanently at compile time with no way to change it
quiz.answer: The client code, which selects and supplies the strategy
quiz.explanation: Strategy selection is external — the client picks which algorithm to plug in.

quiz.question: When is a plain function parameter a better choice than a full Strategy class?
options: When the algorithm is simple, stateless, and fits naturally as a single function
When the algorithm needs several related methods and internal state
When you have ten different complex algorithms to choose from
Never — Strategy classes are always preferable
quiz.answer: When the algorithm is simple, stateless, and fits naturally as a single function
quiz.explanation: A function is often a lighter-weight Strategy for simple, single-operation algorithms.

quiz.question: How does Strategy differ from State?
options: In Strategy, the client chooses the algorithm; in State, the object itself drives transitions between behaviors
They are the same pattern with different names
State can only have one implementation, Strategy can have many
Strategy requires a database, State does not
quiz.answer: In Strategy, the client chooses the algorithm; in State, the object itself drives transitions between behaviors
quiz.explanation: The structural shape is similar, but who controls the swap — and why — is the key distinguishing factor.
